title: Yalta 2.0: A Trump-Xi-Putin summit has little upside for Beijing
gist: Bachulska argues a mooted Trump–Xi–Putin 'Yalta 2.0' trilateral at APEC in Shenzhen (18–19 November 2026) offers little upside for Beijing: it would undercut China's anti-power-politics narrative, pull it into unequal nuclear arms-control framing, and further antagonise a Europe already reeling from a 'second China shock' (record €425bn EU deficit in 2025) and considering tools to restrict China's single-market access.

insights.claim: A potential Trump–Putin–Xi trilateral on the sidelines of APEC in Shenzhen on 18–19 November 2026 was first floated by Moscow; Washington expressed openness mainly on denuclearisation rather than Ukraine, while Beijing stayed tellingly quiet before acknowledging discussions.
insights.speaker: Alicja Bachulska
insights.so_what: Event risk around APEC for Ukraine, arms-control and Europe–China headlines.

insights.claim: 'Yalta 2.0' is impossible because the three powers do not share a strategic calculus and third countries such as wartime Ukraine and Iran have demonstrated their own agency.
insights.speaker: Alicja Bachulska
insights.so_what: Fade expectations of great-power carve-ups resolving conflicts.

insights.claim: Poland's foreign minister Radosław Sikorski said the first Yalta recognised Soviet domination of Eastern Europe, while 'now, Putin wants Ukrainian territories that he can't manage to conquer as a gift'.
insights.speaker: Alicja Bachulska
insights.so_what: Signals strong Eastern European resistance to any deal imposed over Ukraine.

insights.claim: If the trilateral happens it will most likely reiterate positions rather than seek concrete solutions, since Russia wants recognition, the US wants arms control and China wants the broker image without costs or concessions.
insights.speaker: Alicja Bachulska
insights.so_what: Low probability of substantive outcomes; don't trade on a breakthrough.
insights.quote: Russia wants the recognition that comes with the format, the US wants arms control
insights.locator: It will be a very difficult

insights.claim: Optics of a great-power trilateral — even a mere photo-op — could backfire on China by contradicting its decades-long narrative against 'cold war mentality' and 'zero-sum games' that underpins its 'discourse power', explaining Beijing's restraint.
insights.speaker: Alicja Bachulska
insights.so_what: Explains Chinese reticence; lowers odds the meeting materialises.

insights.claim: Beijing resists US-preferred nuclear arms-control talks because, per Tsinghua's Sun Chenghao, a shared reduction framework 'risks turning unequal capabilities into nominally equal responsibilities' given China's smaller arsenal.
insights.speaker: Alicja Bachulska
insights.so_what: Trilateral nuclear arms control unlikely; China's buildup continues.
insights.quote: risks turning unequal capabilities into nominally equal responsibilities

themes.theme: Europe's 'second China shock' and trade-war risk

insights.claim: Europe is confronting a 'second China shock' of industrial overcapacity in advanced, security-relevant goods such as electric vehicles, solar panels, advanced machinery and telecoms, risking deindustrialisation.
insights.speaker: Alicja Bachulska
insights.so_what: Rising EU trade defence risk for Chinese EV/solar exporters; protective tailwind for EU industrials.

insights.claim: The EU trade deficit with China hit a record €425 billion in 2025, with €87 billion reportedly lost from European industry due to unfair Chinese competition, and the BDI branded the situation 'critical'.
insights.speaker: Alicja Bachulska
insights.so_what: Quantifies pressure building toward EU protectionist measures.
insights.quote: EU trade deficit with China hit a record €425 billion in 2025

insights.claim: In October 2026 France and Germany, long divided on China policy, jointly called for a new EU tool allowing immediate restriction of China's access to the single market.
insights.speaker: Alicja Bachulska
insights.so_what: Franco-German alignment materially raises odds of EU market-access restrictions on China.

insights.claim: Europe is preparing for protracted economic competition and potentially a trade war with Beijing, while China needs continued unimpeded access to the European market to channel overcapacity.
insights.speaker: Alicja Bachulska
insights.so_what: EU–China trade war is a live tail risk for Chinese exporters and European autos with China exposure.

insights.claim: Hosting the trilateral would reinforce perceptions that China helps bypass Europe on Ukraine, deepening what Renmin University's Wang Wen called 'strategic anxiety' in Europe and Japan and pushing Europe further down an escalatory path.
insights.speaker: Alicja Bachulska
insights.so_what: Trilateral optics could accelerate EU trade defence against China.
